html:
Proto-Altaic pastoralists is the map's label for the herding peoples of the eastern steppe, in Mongolia, the Altai mountains and around Lake Baikal, from about 1500 to 400 BCE. The name guesses that they were the ancestors of the Turkic, Mongolic and Tungusic peoples. "Altaic" is the old idea that those languages form one family, the Altaic languages; most linguists now doubt it.

What archaeology shows is a world of mounted herders. They kept horses, cattle, sheep and goats and moved between summer and winter pastures. Horses were ridden and sacrificed in great numbers. They left two kinds of monument across Mongolia:

  • Deer stones, standing stones carved with flying deer, from roughly 1200 to 700 BCE.
  • Khirigsuurs, stone burial mounds ringed by smaller mounds holding horse heads.

Later the Slab Grave culture spread across eastern Mongolia. To the west lay the Karasuk people and then the Scythians and Saka. Out of these steppe lands came the Xiongnu, who built the first great steppe empire around 209 BCE.
